system.name: TRAPPIST-1
system.description: Seven Earth-sized rocky planets orbit an ultra-cool red dwarf 40.7 light-years away, three within the habitable zone.

trappist1-star.name: TRAPPIST-1
trappist1-star.description: TRAPPIST-1 is an ultra-cool red dwarf star located 39 light-years from Earth in the constellation Aquarius. It is only slightly larger than Jupiter and burns at roughly 2,566 K, making it one of the coolest known stars to host a multi-planet system.
trappist1-star.funFact: TRAPPIST-1's seven planets were discovered partly by the TRAPPIST telescope in Chile, giving the system its name.

trappist1-b.name: TRAPPIST-1 b
trappist1-b.description: TRAPPIST-1 b is the innermost planet of the system, orbiting extremely close to its host star with a period of just 1.5 days. It is likely tidally locked, keeping one hemisphere in perpetual daytime and the other in eternal night.
trappist1-b.funFact: TRAPPIST-1 b receives about four times as much stellar radiation as Earth receives from the Sun.

trappist1-c.name: TRAPPIST-1 c
trappist1-c.description: TRAPPIST-1 c is the second planet in the system and is similar in size to Earth. It is also likely tidally locked to its star, and recent Webb Space Telescope observations suggest it has little to no thick atmosphere.
trappist1-c.funFact: James Webb Space Telescope observations in 2023 measured TRAPPIST-1 c's thermal emission, suggesting a bare rock or thin CO₂ atmosphere.

trappist1-d.name: TRAPPIST-1 d
trappist1-d.description: TRAPPIST-1 d is the smallest of the seven planets, with a mass about 30% that of Earth. It sits at the inner edge of the system's habitable zone, where liquid water could theoretically exist under the right atmospheric conditions.
trappist1-d.funFact: TRAPPIST-1 d is so close to the habitable zone that it is considered a prime candidate for further atmospheric study.

trappist1-e.name: TRAPPIST-1 e
trappist1-e.description: TRAPPIST-1 e is considered one of the most promising habitable-zone candidates in the system, with an equilibrium temperature close to Earth's. It lies firmly within the habitable zone and has a density suggesting a rocky composition.
trappist1-e.funFact: Among the TRAPPIST-1 planets, TRAPPIST-1 e is often ranked as the most Earth-like in terms of size, density, and insolation.

trappist1-f.name: TRAPPIST-1 f
trappist1-f.description: TRAPPIST-1 f is in the outer habitable zone of the system. Its lower equilibrium temperature suggests that liquid water, if present, would require significant greenhouse warming — making it analogous to a colder Mars-like world.
trappist1-f.funFact: TRAPPIST-1 f receives approximately the same amount of light from its star as Mars receives from the Sun.

trappist1-g.name: TRAPPIST-1 g
trappist1-g.description: TRAPPIST-1 g is the largest planet in the TRAPPIST-1 system, slightly bigger than Earth. At the outer habitable zone boundary, it is likely quite cold, but the gravitational interactions among its neighbors could drive internal heating.
trappist1-g.funFact: The gravitational resonance chain among the TRAPPIST-1 planets means each planet's orbital period is a near-integer ratio of its neighbors.

trappist1-h.name: TRAPPIST-1 h
trappist1-h.description: TRAPPIST-1 h is the outermost and coldest of the seven planets. It is small and likely icy, with equilibrium temperatures well below freezing. It completes the remarkable orbital resonance chain of the whole system.
trappist1-h.funFact: TRAPPIST-1 h's existence was predicted by the resonance chain before it was directly confirmed by the Spitzer Space Telescope.
